cards.reason: One fault: the sense B sentence states a fact about a faith wrongly. 'eating nothing from sunrise to sunset' is not how the Ramadan fast is kept. It begins at dawn (first light), before sunrise, which is why the pre-dawn meal is eaten in the dark, and it also excludes drinking. A Muslim child reading this card would know it is wrong, and a card that misdescribes a religious practice to children is not one I would put in front of a child. Fix only senseB.sentence, for example: 'Many Muslims fast during Ramadan, eating and drinking nothing from first light until sunset.' ('dawn' would also be true; 'first light' keeps every word plainer than the headword). Everything else I checked and would attest as it stands. Sense A: the LIVE key 'swift' (gen-vr-21-same-meaning-21) is a true synonym; slow is its opposite and loud is unrelated. 'asleep' is the item's deliberate 'fast asleep' trap: there fast means deeply, a sense this card does not give, so asleep is not correct under A (quick) or B (go without food). The definition 'moving or doing things very quickly' is true and plain and does not use the headword. The Leo sentence fixes sense A unambiguously as an adjective. wordClass adjective is right for A, verb is right for B. Tier 1 sits with quick, swift and brisk (all tier-1 exemplars). Second sense, weighed hard because it seeds the vocabulary-in-context family: it earns its place. Going without food is a separate meaning, not a stretch, and a 9-11-year-old in the UK genuinely meets it: Ramadan, Lent and Yom Kippur are KS2 RE content, many children have classmates who fast (or fast themselves), and the sense is usable in context ('she was fasting'), which is what the family needs. It is a better choice than 'firmly/deeply' (fast asleep, stuck fast, hold fast), which a child meets almost only inside fixed phrases and which would make 'asleep' a contestable answer on the LIVE item. The definition 'to go without eating for a while' is true, plain and neutral. Framing the sentence on a real community observing its own practice is respectful. likelierKnown A is right: speed is the sense she USES herself every day, not merely the one she sees. Gate: 2 screened, 2 pass (passing is not sufficient here).

Checked against the LIVE key 'timid' (gen-vr-21-same-meaning-25): it is a true synonym of sense A (the timid exemplar reads 'easily frightened and slow to speak up'). No distractor becomes correct: bold is the opposite, polite is about manners, and lonely is about wanting company; the sentence places Ella among people, so it does not lean towards lonely. The definition 'nervous and quiet around people you do not know well' is true and plain, and it does not use the headword. The sentence is one sentence that a child can follow and fixes sense A as an adjective. One sense is right: the verb (a horse shies), 'coconut shy' and 'two shy of ten' are rare in what a 9-11-year-old reads, and 'shy away from' is the same nervous sense. Tier 1 is right and matters because the warm-up hands out tier-1 cards first: shy is an everyday word alongside scared, calm and curious, and it sits below timid (tier 2), the harder synonym the item keys. wordClass adjective is correct. Gate passes.
